newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Iliescu rival sets sights on Romania poll run-off.
newsitem.headline: Iliescu rival sets sights on Romania poll run-off.

text.p: Centrist Emil Constantinescu on Sunday launched the final week of a bitter election campaign to oust ex-Communist President Ion Iliescu with an appeal to sweep away for good the remnants of Romania's Communist rule.

"Fear, lies and theft no longer have any place in Romania. Let them go back where they came from, on the tracks of the tanks which brought them here," Constantinescu told several thousand supporters at a memorial ceremony.
"In a few days, we will be able to say that we have reclaimed our country forever."

Iliescu, who took power in the aftermath of the 1989 upheaval that ousted dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, had a meagre four-point lead over Constantinescu in the first round of the presidential election this month.

But his Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) was routed by Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR) bloc in parliamentary polls. The PDSR has accepted that it will be out of government for the first time in the post-communist era.
The president faces a tough fight in next Sunday's run-off as former Prime Minister Petre Roman, third-place finisher in the opening round, has thrown his support to Constantinescu.

Iliescu's campaign has become increasingly aggressive. He has baldly warned workers and farmers that if elected, Constantinescu will overturn the constitution by bringing back exiled ex-king Michael and allow pre-war landlords to reclaim homes and factories taken over in communist times.
"Workers, farmers, tenants, Romanians, beware!" Iliescu's latest campaign clip warns television viewers. "You'll lose your jobs, your land, your homes. The country could break up."

In his speech marking the death a year ago of Peasant Party leader Corneliu Coposu, jailed for 17 years under Communist rule, Constantinescu said the president was becoming desperate to stave off defeat.
"These attacks stem from despair and fear," he told Reuters after the ceremony next to a bronze bust of Coposu, opposite the former Communist party building fled by Ceausescu in 1989.
"They will only push more and more Romanians to vote for those guaranteeing stability, reconciliation and prosperity."

Final results of the parliamentary vote showed both Iliescu and Constantinescu won seats in the upper house, the Senate. Prime Minister Nicolae Vacaroiu and 16 members of his cabinet, all likely to be thrown out of office, were also elected.

Constantinescu blames Iliescu's reluctant reforms for casting millions of Romanians into poverty and proposes a 200-day programme to jump-start the economy and catch up with ex-communist states Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland.
He says Romania can only shake off Communist rule if the Moscow-educated president, who held various top posts under Ceausescu, is thrown out of office.
Iliescu says Constantinescu, an academic who had no political career under Communism, is not up to the job.
He promises to work with the new government and depicts himself as the sole guarantee against excesses by rightist politicians controlling parliament and the new cabinet.
"The presidency is too big a hat for Constantinescu to wear," he told a weekend rally in the Danube town of Braila.
The two meet head-on in television debates this week.
Iliescu, elected in 1990 and 1992, has lost much of his support in Romania's cities and opinion surveys show he relies increasingly on older and less educated rural voters.
"It is a question of psychology," the president told reporters last week. "Perhaps simple people have more intuiton. It's a feeling that I'm a guy close to them."
